metadata.narrative: Imagine that a future technology can erase specific memories without side effects. Craft a detailed policy brief that takes a stance on whether courts can mandate the procedure for violent offenders to prevent the likelihood of re-offense. Justify your response via arguments surrounding deontology, consequentialism, and three relevant historical precedents with citations.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Courts should not be empowered to mandate memory erasure for violent offenders, even where the procedure is technically free of physical side effects, though they may permissibly offer it as one voluntary alternative within a broader sentencing or civil-commitment scheme.

This brief grounds that stance in deontological respect for personal autonomy and mental integrity, in consequentialist concerns about predictive error and mission creep, and in three historical precedents that map closely onto the proposed intervention.

From a deontological standpoint, Kantian retributivism holds that punishment is justified only insofar as it treats the offender as a rational, autonomous agent punished for what he has done, not manipulated as a means to some future social benefit.

Compelling an offender to undergo an irreversible alteration of his own memories to serve society's interest in reduced recidivism treats him instrumentally, as an object to be reengineered rather than a person to be justly punished.

Protective and victim-vindication theories of retribution similarly hold that offenders possess a "right to be punished" as morally culpable agents, a right undermined if the state instead reshapes their minds to preempt future wrongdoing.

Emerging neuroethics scholarship reinforces this by proposing a right to cognitive liberty, mental privacy, mental integrity, and psychological continuity, explicitly naming memory engineering and selective memory erasure as paradigm threats to these rights when imposed without consent.

Commentators note that no existing constitutional or statutory framework currently grants individuals explicit sovereignty over their own brains, so courts adjudicating compelled memory erasure would operate in a legal vacuum rather than settled doctrine.

Neuroethics literature on memory-dampening technologies also raises a "duty to remember," particularly for witnesses and perpetrators whose memories serve evidentiary and historical functions that coerced erasure would permanently destroy.

Consequentialist analysis complicates but does not overturn this conclusion, since a purely aggregative calculus might endorse mandatory erasure if it reliably reduced victimization, incapacitated dangerous impulses, and lowered the fiscal burden of incarceration.

Yet consequentialist punishment theory itself warns that policies justified by predicted future dangerousness routinely produce false positives and negatives, meaning some offenders would be forcibly altered despite posing little real risk of reoffending.

The same theory criticizes incapacitation-based sentencing for punishing people preemptively for offenses not yet committed, a critique applying with even greater force to erasure imposed on statistical risk rather than proven volitional impairment.

Even sympathetic utilitarian arguments about memory-altering technology, drawn from debates over propranolol and traumatic memory, concede that mitigating victim harm does not automatically justify compelling defendants to undergo irreversible neural interventions whose downstream effects remain poorly understood.

Three historical precedents illuminate how courts have previously handled state-mandated bodily and mental interventions justified by future risk, and each counsels caution toward a compulsory memory-erasure regime.

The first, Buck v. Bell (1927), upheld Virginia's compulsory sterilization of Carrie Buck on the rationale that removing her reproductive capacity would protect society from "unfit" offspring, a decision later shown to rest on fabricated evidence and to have opened the door to mass eugenic sterilization of over sixty thousand Americans.

Buck v. Bell shows how a consequentialist appeal to societal welfare can override individual bodily autonomy when courts defer to expert claims about future dangerousness, and its repudiation warns directly against compelling irreversible neural alteration on similarly speculative risk assessments.

The second precedent, Kansas v. Hendricks (1997) together with its limiting companion Kansas v. Crane (2002), establishes that the state may civilly commit sexually violent offenders based on a mental abnormality and likelihood of reoffense, but only where it also proves genuine volitional impairment rather than merely a predicted statistical risk.

This doctrine matters because it shows that even where courts permit preventive intervention keyed to future violence, they have refused to authorize it on prediction alone, instead requiring individualized proof of impaired self-control, a threshold a categorical erasure mandate for all violent offenders would not satisfy.

The civil commitment framework also required detailed due-process protections, including counsel, cross-examination, and periodic review, none of which map cleanly onto a one-time, irreversible procedure that cannot be revisited if a risk assessment later proves wrong.

The third precedent, the trilogy of Washington v. Harper, Sell v. United States, and Riggins v. Nevada, establishes that prisoners and defendants retain a significant liberty interest against forced medical intervention, permitting involuntary treatment only under narrowly defined policies and limited purposes, never merely for state convenience.

Sell imposed stringent limits on forcibly medicating a defendant solely to restore trial competence, and Riggins recognized a right to refuse psychiatric medication even during trial, signaling that courts treat compelled alteration of mental states as constitutionally suspect even where clear governmental interests exist.

Read together, these precedents suggest any court-mandated erasure regime would need the volitional-impairment showing required under Hendricks and Crane and the narrow-tailoring safeguards required under Harper, Sell, and Riggins, while still risking the fabricated-science overreach that discredited Buck v. Bell.

Balancing the deontological objection to instrumentalizing offenders' minds against the consequentialist appeal of recidivism reduction, this brief recommends that memory erasure be authorized only as a voluntary alternative sentence or commitment condition to which an offender consents with full information and independent counsel, never as a court-imposed mandate.

Courts adopting this voluntary model should require the same individualized volitional-impairment findings used in sexually-violent-predator proceedings and the narrow-tailoring analysis used in the forced-medication line, so the state cannot substitute prediction-based mandates for the proven-danger standard already developed in law.

Policymakers should also heed the neuroethics warning that legislating here without first codifying rights to cognitive liberty and mental integrity would leave courts without a doctrinal anchor, inviting the kind of unreviewed overreach that produced Buck v. Bell's discredited sterilizations.

In sum, a future memory-erasure technology may eventually earn a limited, consent-based place in criminal justice as a rehabilitative option, but deontological respect for personal identity, consequentialist skepticism of risk-based mandates, and the cautionary history of Buck v. Bell, Hendricks and Crane, and the Harper-Sell-Riggins trilogy together counsel against ever making it compulsory.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

From a deontological standpoint, Kantian retributivism holds that punishment is justified only insofar as it treats the offender as a rational, autonomous agent punished for what he has done, not manipulated as a means to some future social benefit.

Compelling an offender to undergo an irreversible alteration of his own memories to serve society's interest in reduced recidivism treats him instrumentally, as an object to be reengineered rather than a person to be justly punished.

Protective and victim-vindication theories of retribution similarly hold that offenders possess a "right to be punished" as morally culpable agents, a right undermined if the state instead reshapes their minds to preempt future wrongdoing.

Emerging neuroethics scholarship reinforces this by proposing a right to cognitive liberty, mental privacy, mental integrity, and psychological continuity, explicitly naming memory engineering and selective memory erasure as paradigm threats to these rights when imposed without consent.

Commentators note that no existing constitutional or statutory framework currently grants individuals explicit sovereignty over their own brains, so courts adjudicating compelled memory erasure would operate in a legal vacuum rather than settled doctrine.

Neuroethics literature on memory-dampening technologies also raises a "duty to remember," particularly for witnesses and perpetrators whose memories serve evidentiary and historical functions that coerced erasure would permanently destroy.

Consequentialist analysis complicates but does not overturn this conclusion, since a purely aggregative calculus might endorse mandatory erasure if it reliably reduced victimization, incapacitated dangerous impulses, and lowered the fiscal burden of incarceration.

Yet consequentialist punishment theory itself warns that policies justified by predicted future dangerousness routinely produce false positives and negatives, meaning some offenders would be forcibly altered despite posing little real risk of reoffending.

The same theory criticizes incapacitation-based sentencing for punishing people preemptively for offenses not yet committed, a critique applying with even greater force to erasure imposed on statistical risk rather than proven volitional impairment.

Even sympathetic utilitarian arguments about memory-altering technology, drawn from debates over propranolol and traumatic memory, concede that mitigating victim harm does not automatically justify compelling defendants to undergo irreversible neural interventions whose downstream effects remain poorly understood.

Three historical precedents illuminate how courts have previously handled state-mandated bodily and mental interventions justified by future risk, and each counsels caution toward a compulsory memory-erasure regime.

The first, Buck v. Bell (1927), upheld Virginia's compulsory sterilization of Carrie Buck on the rationale that removing her reproductive capacity would protect society from "unfit" offspring, a decision later shown to rest on fabricated evidence and to have opened the door to mass eugenic sterilization of over sixty thousand Americans.

Buck v. Bell shows how a consequentialist appeal to societal welfare can override individual bodily autonomy when courts defer to expert claims about future dangerousness, and its repudiation warns directly against compelling irreversible neural alteration on similarly speculative risk assessments.

The second precedent, Kansas v. Hendricks (1997) together with its limiting companion Kansas v. Crane (2002), establishes that the state may civilly commit sexually violent offenders based on a mental abnormality and likelihood of reoffense, but only where it also proves genuine volitional impairment rather than merely a predicted statistical risk.

This doctrine matters because it shows that even where courts permit preventive intervention keyed to future violence, they have refused to authorize it on prediction alone, instead requiring individualized proof of impaired self-control, a threshold a categorical erasure mandate for all violent offenders would not satisfy.

The civil commitment framework also required detailed due-process protections, including counsel, cross-examination, and periodic review, none of which map cleanly onto a one-time, irreversible procedure that cannot be revisited if a risk assessment later proves wrong.

The third precedent, the trilogy of Washington v. Harper, Sell v. United States, and Riggins v. Nevada, establishes that prisoners and defendants retain a significant liberty interest against forced medical intervention, permitting involuntary treatment only under narrowly defined policies and limited purposes, never merely for state convenience.

Read together, these precedents suggest any court-mandated erasure regime would need the volitional-impairment showing required under Hendricks and Crane and the narrow-tailoring safeguards required under Harper, Sell, and Riggins, while still risking the fabricated-science overreach that discredited Buck v. Bell.

Policymakers should also heed the neuroethics warning that legislating here without first codifying rights to cognitive liberty and mental integrity would leave courts without a doctrinal anchor, inviting the kind of unreviewed overreach that produced Buck v. Bell's discredited sterilizations.

Bell, Hendricks and Crane, and the Harper-Sell-Riggins trilogy together counsel against ever making it compulsory.
